title: Best Student Privacy & Campus Surveillance Tools Compared
metaDescription: Signal, DuckDuckGo, Tor Browser and Proton VPN compared for students on tracking, school networks and exams, scored on one published rubric.
intro: Students face digital surveillance from proctoring software, school-issued devices and campus network monitoring. This page compares four privacy tools students use on the same six criteria, including how well each works on school networks and during exams.

verdict.summary: On these six criteria Signal scores highest, though it is rated on only four of them because two don't apply to a messaging app: it is free, easy to use and end-to-end encrypted, and school network monitoring can't read its messages. DuckDuckGo is a close second: its search engine doesn't track you, its browser and extension block known trackers, and it works on school networks without special setup. Tor Browser comes next: it offers strong anonymity but is slower than a regular browser and often blocked or flagged on campus networks. Proton VPN scores lowest: it hides your traffic from the network but is usually blocked during online exams and may break school rules. On a school-issued device, assume the school can see what you do, whichever tool you use.

bestFor.reason: Highest score here: end-to-end encryption keeps message content from network monitoring
Close second here: its browser and extension block known trackers, it works on school networks and it is free
Strong privacy protection when using public Wi-Fi or home networks

pro_tips: Always read your school's acceptable use policy before installing privacy tools - some institutions prohibit VPNs but allow other browsers and search engines.
Create separate user accounts on your personal devices for school work and personal use to compartmentalize your digital footprint.

Use DuckDuckGo as your default search engine even on school devices - it's usually allowed and doesn't keep a search history tied to you, though monitoring software on the device can still see your searches.
Enable two-factor authentication on all your educational accounts to prevent unauthorized access to your academic records.
Review and limit the permissions you grant to educational apps - many collect far more data than necessary for their core function.

faqs.question: Can I use a VPN during online exams?
faqs.answer: Most proctoring software blocks VPNs and may flag them as suspicious. Many proctoring systems also require a specific browser, such as a lockdown browser or Chrome with a proctoring extension, so check your exam guidelines and use exactly what they specify.

faqs.question: Will privacy tools affect my grades or academic standing?
faqs.answer: Privacy tools that comply with school policies should not affect your grades. However, avoid using tools that circumvent academic integrity measures or violate your institution's technology policies.

faqs.question: What data can schools legally collect about students?
faqs.answer: Under FERPA, schools can collect educational records and directory information. However, many edtech companies collect additional data. Review privacy policies and opt out of non-essential data collection when possible.

faqs.question: How do I protect my privacy on school-issued devices?
faqs.answer: Assume school IT can see what you do on a school-issued device, whichever browser you use: device-management and monitoring software can record activity outside the browser. Avoid logging into personal accounts on it and keep personal activities on your own devices.

faqs.question: Are free privacy tools as effective as paid ones?
faqs.answer: Many free tools, like DuckDuckGo and Signal, give strong privacy protection. Paid tools often add features or wider coverage. Start with free options and pay only for something you need.
